title: The Hidden Cost of Cutting Forests
paragraphs: Forests cover roughly a third of the planet's land surface, yet they are shrinking at an alarming pace. Every year, [[logging-1|commercial logging]] companies [[fell-1|fell]] millions of trees to supply timber for construction, furniture and paper. In many tropical regions, [[deforestation-1|deforestation rates]] have risen sharply over the past fifty years, and scientists warn that the [[impact-1|environmental impact]] of this activity reaches far beyond the loss of the trees themselves.

A healthy forest supports [[array-1|a vast array of]] living things. Within a single hectare of rainforest, researchers have recorded hundreds of tree species and [[myriad-1|myriad]] insects, fungi and birds. When the canopy is removed, these [[terrestrial-1|terrestrial species]] lose their [[habitat-1|natural habitats]] almost overnight. Some are able to move to neighbouring woodland, but many cannot, and populations that once seemed secure can [[vanish-1|vanish completely]] within a few decades.

The damage also affects the ground beneath the trees. Leaves and branches [[intercept-1|intercept rainfall]], slowing its fall so that water soaks gently into the earth. Roots, meanwhile, bind the soil together and help [[stabilize-1|stabilize]] steep slopes. Once the forest is cleared, heavy rain strikes bare land directly, and [[erosion-1|soil erosion]] accelerates. Valuable [[nutrient-1|soil nutrients]] are washed away, which [[inhibit-1|inhibits the growth]] of new [[vegetation-1|vegetation]] and leaves the land far less productive than before.

Rivers and lakes suffer as well. Mud carried downhill clouds the water, blocking the sunlight that [[aquatic-1|aquatic plants]] need to survive. Fish and other forms of [[aquatic-1|aquatic life]] may struggle to breathe or feed, and in some cases the sediment [[extend-1|extends]] many kilometres downstream. Fuel spills from heavy machinery and chemicals used to treat timber add further [[pollution-1|water pollution]], harming communities that depend on these rivers for drinking water and food.

Forests are also a vital [[defense-1|defense against]] climate change. Trees absorb carbon dioxide and store it for centuries, so large-scale clearing releases greenhouse gases and weakens one of the planet's most effective natural safeguards. Surrounding villages may lose their [[defense-1|first line of defense]] against floods and landslides, too.

Fortunately, solutions exist. Governments can tighten rules against [[logging-1|illegal logging]], and consumers can choose products from certified sources where only selected trees are removed. Replanting programmes, if carefully managed, help restore damaged land. Protecting the [[environment-1|natural environment]] is not simply a matter of saving attractive scenery; it is essential for clean water, fertile soil and a stable climate for future generations.

title: Journeys Across the Globe: The Science of Bird Migration
paragraphs: Each autumn, billions of birds leave the places where they spent the summer and set off on journeys that may cover thousands of kilometres. This [[migration-2|seasonal migration]] has [[fascinate-2|fascinated scientists]] for centuries, and even a [[observer-2|casual observer]] watching geese fly overhead in a V-shaped formation can sense that something remarkable is taking place.

The main reason birds travel is food. Many [[species-2|species of bird]] [[breed-2|breed]] in the far north of the [[hemisphere-2|northern hemisphere]], where long summer days produce enormous numbers of insects for hungry chicks. When winter approaches, however, these areas become cold and empty, so the birds head south to regions that offer [[optimal-2|optimal conditions]] for feeding. Some, like the Arctic tern, even cross into the [[hemisphere-2|southern hemisphere]], enjoying two summers every year.

Such journeys demand careful preparation. Before departure, birds eat far more than usual and store fat, which acts as [[fuel-2|fuel for the journey]]. A small songbird may nearly double its body weight in just a few weeks. During the flight, many birds [[endure-2|endure harsh conditions]], including storms, cold and lack of food, while crossing deserts, oceans and [[windswept-2|windswept islands]] where there is almost nowhere to rest. For a creature weighing less than twenty grams, completing such a trip is [[feat-2|a remarkable feat]].

Perhaps the most puzzling [[aspect-2|aspect]] of migration is [[navigation-2|navigation]]. Research suggests that birds have [[evolve-2|evolved]] several methods of finding their way. [[diurnal-2|Diurnal species]], which fly during daylight, use the position of the sun, while [[nocturnal-2|nocturnal species]] appear to rely on the pattern of stars. Many birds can also sense the Earth's magnetic field, and some recognise landmarks such as coastlines and mountain ranges. When clouds [[obscure-2|obscure the sun]] or stars, the magnetic sense seems to become especially important.

Even so, mistakes happen. Young birds on their first journey sometimes [[stray-2|stray off course]] and turn up hundreds of kilometres from their usual route, to the delight of birdwatchers. Strong winds can also push flocks far out to sea.

Today, migrating birds face new dangers. Wetlands and forests that they [[inhabit-2|inhabit]] along their routes are being drained or cleared, and bright city lights can confuse birds that fly at night. Because many populations are declining, conservationists argue that [[imperative-2|it is imperative that]] countries work together to protect stopover sites, since a bird that crosses a dozen borders depends on every one of them.

title: Surviving the Sea of Sand: Plants of the Taklimakan
paragraphs: The Taklimakan Desert in north-western China is one of the largest sandy deserts in the world. Its name is often translated as 'the place you enter but cannot leave', and for good reason. Rainfall is [[sparse-3|sparse]], often less than 40 millimetres a year, while [[extreme-3|extreme temperatures]] range from over 40°C in summer to below minus 20°C in winter. [[violent-3|Violent winds]] regularly lift huge clouds of sand, burying anything in their path. At first sight, it seems impossible that anything could grow here.

Nevertheless, a small but [[diverse-3|diverse range of]] plants has [[adapt-3|adapted to]] these harsh conditions. Most of them [[occupy-3|occupy]] the [[fringe-3|fringes of the desert]], where rivers flowing from the surrounding mountains bring some water. These edges form a [[transitional-3|transitional zone]] between the empty dunes of the centre and the farmland and oases beyond. Scientists studying this zone want to [[determine-3|determine]] exactly how the plants survive, because the knowledge may help protect other dry regions.

Water is the most serious [[stressor-3|environmental stressor]], and desert plants have developed several [[mechanism-3|survival mechanisms]] to deal with it. The tamarisk shrub, for example, sends roots more than ten metres down to reach underground water. Other species have small, waxy leaves that [[minimize-3|minimize water loss]] by reducing [[evaporation-3|evaporation]] from their surfaces. Some plants [[accumulate-3|accumulate]] salt in their tissues, which helps them draw [[moisture-3|moisture]] from dry, salty soil, and they can later shed the salt through special glands. Where groundwater is very salty, rare floods may even [[dilute-3|dilute]] it enough for young plants to establish themselves.

Temperature is another challenge. The daily [[swing-3|temperature swing]] in the Taklimakan can exceed 20 degrees, which would damage the cells of many ordinary plants. Desert species, however, are [[resilient-3|remarkably resilient]]. The poplar tree known as the Euphrates poplar can survive years of drought, losing branches in bad seasons and growing new ones when conditions improve.

Reproduction is also carefully timed. Because rainfall is unpredictable, many desert plants are [[prolific-3|prolific]] seed producers, releasing thousands of seeds that can wait in the sand for years. When a rare shower arrives, they germinate quickly and complete their life cycle in a few weeks.

These plants do more than [[thrive-3|thrive in]] a hostile place; they also protect it. Their roots hold the sand in place and slow the spread of the desert towards nearby towns. For this reason, local authorities now plant tamarisk and other species along highways, hoping that these tough survivors will act as a living barrier against the moving dunes.

title: Seeing Without Looking: Peripheral Vision in Sport
paragraphs: When people talk about good eyesight, they usually mean the ability to read small letters or recognise a face at a distance. In sport, however, another kind of [[vision-4|vision]] can be just as important. [[peripheral-4|Peripheral vision]] is the ability to see objects at the edges of our [[range-4|range of vision]], outside the small central area on which we [[focus-4|focus our eyes]]. Although the images it produces are often [[indistinct-4|indistinct]], this wider view allows players to notice what is happening around them without turning their heads.

Consider a basketball player running down the court. Her eyes may be fixed on the basket, but at the [[boundary-4|boundary]] of her sight she is aware of a teammate moving into space and a defender closing in. To her, these figures may appear only as [[blur-4|a blur of colour]], yet the brain can [[detect-4|detect movement]] extremely quickly. Much of this processing happens [[unconsciously-4|unconsciously]], so the player can [[coordinate-4|coordinate her movements]] and pass the ball before she has consciously decided to do so.

Research has [[demonstrate-4|clearly demonstrated]] that [[athlete-4|elite athletes]] use their peripheral vision more effectively than beginners. In one experiment, experienced footballers and novices watched video clips while their eye movements were recorded. The experts tended to fix their gaze on a central point and use their side vision to [[scan-4|scan the area]] around it, whereas the novices moved their eyes constantly from player to player. As a result, the experts were better able to [[anticipate-4|anticipate the movement]] of opponents and choose the right moment for a pass or tackle.

Several factors can [[complicate-4|complicate matters]]. Fatigue and anxiety tend to narrow the visual field, a problem sometimes called 'tunnel vision'. Crowds, flashing advertising boards and other [[distracting-4|distracting]] elements can also reduce concentration. Top players learn to [[tolerate-4|tolerate]] this pressure and filter out what is irrelevant. Moreover, the [[range-4|range]] of peripheral awareness can shrink [[indiscernibly-4|indiscernibly]] as a match goes on, so that a tired defender may not notice the danger until it is too late.

The good news is that this skill can be trained. Coaches now use drills in which players must react to lights or signals appearing at the edge of their sight while carrying out a [[maneuver-4|complex maneuver]]. Video games and virtual reality systems are also being tested. Early results suggest that such training can [[performance-4|improve performance]], particularly in fast team sports where the ball and players change position every second. In short, the best athletes are not only those who see clearly, but also those who see widely.

title: From Roman Arenas to the Big Top: A Short History of the Circus
paragraphs: The word 'circus' comes from Latin and means 'circle' or 'ring'. In [[ancient-5|ancient times]], the Circus Maximus in Rome was a [[massive-5|massive]] stadium where as many as 150,000 [[spectator-5|spectators]] gathered to watch chariot races. The Romans also [[exhibit-5|exhibited]] [[exotic-5|exotic animals]] such as lions and elephants brought from distant parts of their empire. Today, only a few [[remnant-5|remnants]] of this great [[venue-5|venue]] [[survive-5|survive to this day]], but visitors can still imagine its former [[grandeur-5|grandeur]].

The modern circus, however, has a much shorter history. It was [[found-5|founded]] in London in 1768 by Philip Astley, a former cavalry officer with [[talent-5|a talent for]] trick riding. Astley discovered that if he galloped in a circle, the force helped him stay balanced while standing on the horse's back. He built a ring about thirteen metres across, a size still used in many circuses, and soon added jugglers, acrobats and clowns to fill the gaps between his riding displays. A small [[band-5|band]] played music to excite the crowd.

During the nineteenth [[century-5|century]], the circus [[develop-5|developed rapidly]] into one of the most [[popular-5|popular]] [[entertainment-5|forms of entertainment]] in Europe and North America. In the United States, companies began touring with enormous canvas tents known as 'big tops', which allowed them to perform in small towns that had no theatre. Trains carried performers, equipment and animals from one place to the next, and the arrival of the circus was often a major local event. Some companies eventually [[permanently-5|permanently]] settled in purpose-built buildings, while others remained on the road.

Animal acts played a central role. Skilled [[trainer-5|animal trainers]] taught horses, bears and even tigers to perform tricks, and audiences were amazed by these displays. In the late twentieth century, however, public attitudes began to change. Campaigners argued that travelling life caused suffering to wild animals, and many countries passed laws to ban or [[reduce-5|significantly reduce]] their use in shows.

As a result, the circus has had to reinvent itself. Contemporary companies focus on human skill, combining acrobatics with dance, theatre and striking lighting. Instead of animals, they emphasise storytelling and artistic design, attracting new audiences who might never have attended a traditional show. Meanwhile, several historic circus buildings in Europe have undergone [[renovation-5|major renovation]] and now host both performances and museum collections, ensuring that this colourful tradition continues for another generation.

title: Rethinking Free Time: What We Do When We Are Not Working
paragraphs: For much of history, leisure was a luxury enjoyed by a small minority. Today, most adults in developed countries have several hours of free time each week, yet they often spend [[chunk-6|a large chunk of]] it in front of a screen. Researchers are increasingly asking whether the way people use this time matters, and the [[overwhelming-6|overwhelming evidence]] suggests that it does.

The most [[obvious-6|obvious]] concern is health. Watching television or scrolling through social media is a [[passive-6|passive activity]] that burns very little energy. When such habits replace sport or walking, people are more likely to put on weight, and many experts link the rise in [[obesity-6|rates of obesity]] to sedentary leisure. It is [[acknowledge-6|widely acknowledged]] that regular [[physical-6|physical activity]] reduces the risk of heart disease and helps people live longer.

Free time also affects the mind. A [[authority-6|leading authority on]] well-being, the psychologist Martin Seligman, has argued that people feel most satisfied when they are absorbed in challenging tasks. Activities that require concentration, such as playing a musical instrument, learning a language or solving puzzles, provide [[intellectual-6|intellectual stimulation]] and can help people [[rejuvenate-6|feel rejuvenated]] after a stressful week. By contrast, those who [[merely-6|merely watch]] others perform may gain less lasting satisfaction.

Social contact is another [[crucial-6|crucial factor]]. Team sports, clubs and volunteering allow people to [[engage-6|engage in]] shared activities and build friendships. Studies indicate that individuals who [[suffer-6|suffer from]] loneliness are at greater risk of [[depression-6|depression]], and a regular group [[pastime-6|pastime]] can protect against this. Taking part in such groups also gives people a safe way to express their [[emotion-6|emotions]], whether through laughter, competition or creative work.

Nevertheless, many people are [[reluctant-6|reluctant to change]] their routines. After a long day, it may feel easier to sit on the sofa than to go to the gym. Some particularly [[industrious-6|industrious]] workers even feel guilty about relaxing at all, seeing leisure as wasted time. Psychologists suggest that the solution is not to fill every free moment with activity, but to plan leisure [[deliberately-6|deliberately]], choosing a balance of rest, movement and mental challenge.

Governments and employers can help as well. Well-maintained parks, affordable sports centres and flexible working hours make it easier for people to choose active pursuits. Ultimately, how we spend our free time is a personal decision, but understanding its effects can help us make choices that benefit both body and mind.

title: Lighting the Way: The Story of Early Headlamps
paragraphs: Long before electric bulbs existed, people who travelled at night faced a [[tricky-7|tricky problem]]: how could they see what lay ahead? For the drivers of horse-drawn carriages, a dark road was a potential [[disaster-7|disaster]], since a hidden ditch or a fallen branch could overturn a vehicle in seconds. The earliest solution was a simple candle lantern fixed to the side of a coach, but such lanterns [[cast-7|cast]] only a weak glow and were easily blown out by the wind. Travellers on foot were even more [[vulnerable-7|vulnerable]], relying on [[portable-7|portable]] oil lamps that lit little more than the path beneath their feet.

The railways brought the first serious [[innovation-7|innovation]] in forward lighting. In the nineteenth century, a [[locomotive-7|steam locomotive]] pulling a heavy [[freight-7|freight train]] through the night needed [[illuminator-7|a powerful illuminator]] so that the driver could spot obstacles on the track in time. Engineers [[equip-7|equipped]] engines with large oil lamps placed in front of a curved metal [[reflector-7|reflector]], which gathered the light and sent it forward in a narrow beam. Similar lamps were fitted to ships, where crews [[knot-7|sailing at ten knots]] through fog needed to see buoys and warn other vessels of their position.

When the motor car appeared at the end of the nineteenth century, manufacturers borrowed these ideas. The first car headlamps burned acetylene gas, which was [[generate-7|generated]] inside the lamp when water dripped slowly onto a chemical called calcium carbide. The flame produced an [[intense-7|intense light]] that was far brighter than anything oil could offer. However, the system had [[drawback-7|a major drawback]]: drivers had to refill the chemicals regularly, and lighting the lamps in wet or windy weather required considerable patience.

Electric headlamps, introduced around 1898, eventually replaced gas. Early versions were not very [[efficient-7|efficient]], because the small batteries of the time quickly ran flat on long journeys. The real breakthrough came in the 1910s, when cars began to carry their own engine-driven dynamos, which supplied a steady current. Lamps also had to be [[rugged-7|rugged]] enough to survive rough roads and constant vibration, and before long they became a standard feature that dealers proudly put [[display-7|on display]] in their showroom windows.

As the car became the dominant [[mode-7|mode of transport]], governments introduced [[stringent-7|stringent safety regulations]]. Drivers complained about the glare from oncoming vehicles, so new laws required dipped beams that [[cast-7|cast light]] downwards onto the road. Today, [[efficient-7|highly efficient]] LED lamps use a fraction of the energy of their ancestors, and some modern vehicles can even [[display-7|display information]] on the road surface ahead. Yet the basic principle, a bright source combined with a carefully shaped mirror, has changed remarkably little in more than a century.

title: Beneath the Streets: Europe's Great Metro Systems
paragraphs: By the middle of the nineteenth century, the streets of London were so [[clog-8|clogged with traffic]] that crossing the city could take hours. Horses, carts and crowds of [[pedestrian-8|pedestrians]] fought for space on narrow roads. The solution, which many considered absurd at the time, was to build a railway below the [[surface-8|surface]]. In 1863 the Metropolitan Railway [[operation-8|came into operation]], becoming the world's first [[underground-8|underground railway]]. Its steam engines [[release-8|released]] thick smoke into the tunnels, so engineers had to build large [[vent-8|vents]] along the route to let the dirty air escape.

Construction itself was [[disruptive-8|highly disruptive]]. The earliest lines were built using the so-called cut-and-cover method, in which workers dug a deep trench along a street, laid the tracks and then roofed it over. This caused [[destruction-8|the destruction of]] roads and even houses, and traffic had to be diverted for months. Later, tunnelling machines allowed engineers to dig much deeper, leaving life at street level largely undisturbed and [[shield-8|shielding]] residents from much of the noise and vibration.

Other capitals soon followed. Budapest opened continental Europe's first underground line in 1896, and Paris launched its Métro in 1900. The Paris authorities quickly [[expand-8|expanded the network]], and within a few decades almost every part of the city lay within a short walk of a station. New shops and cafés [[spring-up-8|sprang up around]] the entrances, many of which were [[decorate-8|decorated with]] elegant iron and glass designs by the architect Hector Guimard. These curving Art Nouveau entrances remain one of the most recognisable features of Parisian [[architecture-8|architecture]].

Moscow took a different approach. When its metro opened in 1935, the stations were designed to [[showcase-8|showcase]] the achievements of the state. Marble walls, chandeliers and mosaics allowed them to [[rival-8|rival]] the finest palaces, and grand halls such as Komsomolskaya became [[centerpiece-8|the centerpiece of]] the system. For its planners, beauty was [[intrinsic-8|intrinsic to]] the project: the metro was meant to be not only a means of travel but also a symbol of national pride. During the Second World War, deep stations served as bomb shelters, and one was even used as a military [[headquarters-8|headquarters]].

Today, Europe's metros face new challenges. Growing populations mean that operators must [[utilize-8|utilize space]] as cleverly as possible, extending platforms and running driverless trains at shorter intervals. Powerful ventilation systems [[release-8|release heat]] that builds up from brakes and crowded carriages, and wide [[pedestrian-8|pedestrian]] tunnels link different lines to make changing trains easier. Whether they are admired for their art or simply for their speed, these hidden networks remain the quiet heart of city life.

title: Charging Ahead: The Global Rise of the Electric Car
paragraphs: Electric vehicles are hardly a new idea. In the late nineteenth century, battery-powered cars were quiet, clean and easy to drive, and they had a strong [[appeal-9|appeal]] for wealthy city residents. However, their range was limited, and once petrol engines became cheaper and more powerful, electric models fell out of use. For most of the twentieth century, progress in the field was [[plodding-9|slow and plodding]], and the electric car was [[classify-9|classified as]] little more than a curiosity.

This situation changed [[markedly-9|markedly]] in the early twenty-first century. Concern about air quality in [[urban-9|urban areas]], where [[fume-9|exhaust fumes]] from millions of vehicles damage public health, pushed governments to look for alternatives. At the same time, improvements in lithium-ion batteries meant that a car could travel several hundred kilometres on a single [[charge-9|charge]]. Designers also began to give electric models real [[flair-9|flair]], proving that environmentally friendly vehicles did not have to look dull.

Governments have played a key role in [[accelerate-9|accelerating change]]. Norway offers perhaps the clearest example: by removing heavy purchase taxes and allowing electric cars to use bus lanes, it created a powerful [[monetary-9|monetary]] [[incentive-9|incentive to]] switch. As a result, the vast majority of new cars sold there are now electric. China, meanwhile, has [[embrace-9|embraced the technology]] as part of its industrial strategy and has become the world's largest market for battery vehicles.

Nevertheless, several factors continue to [[hamper-9|hamper growth]]. [[charge-9|Charging stations]] are still scarce in many [[rural-9|rural communities]], where drivers cover long distances and have few alternatives. Buyers also worry about the [[span-9|life span]] of batteries and the high cost of replacing them. In countries where [[standard-9|living standards]] are lower, the purchase price remains the biggest barrier of all. Moreover, where electricity comes mainly from coal, an electric car may [[consume-9|consume energy]] that is far from clean.

Patterns of use also differ from place to place. In [[suburban-9|suburban areas]], where many households have a garage, owners can simply [[charge-9|charge]] their cars overnight. By contrast, people living in apartment blocks in city centres depend on public chargers. Planners point out that [[sprawl-9|urban sprawl]] makes car ownership almost essential for many families, so electrification is particularly valuable for the daily [[commuter-9|commuter]] who drives long distances from the outskirts. As batteries grow cheaper, many analysts expect the electric car to become the [[standard-9|standard]] choice for drivers worldwide.

title: From Clay to Script: How Writing Began
paragraphs: Writing is one of the most important inventions in human history, yet no single [[creator-10|creator]] can be named for it. Most [[scholar-10|scholars believe]] that it developed gradually and independently in several parts of the world. The earliest known system appeared in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, more than five thousand years ago, and its development is closely linked to [[civilization-10|the rise of civilization]] in that region.

The story begins with farming. When people began to [[settle-10|settle permanently]] in fertile river valleys, they formed [[agricultural-10|agricultural societies]] that produced a surplus of grain and livestock. This surplus had to be stored, traded and counted, and communities needed a reliable way of recording who owned what. According to the archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat, the answer lay in small [[token-10|clay tokens]] of different shapes, each of which stood for a particular item, such as a jar of oil or a sheep.

Over time, these tokens were sealed inside hollow clay balls to guarantee a deal, and their shapes were pressed onto the outside. Eventually, officials realised that the marks alone were enough. They began to [[inscribe-10|inscribe]] signs directly onto flat [[tablet-10|clay tablets]] with a sharpened reed, producing the wedge-shaped script now known as cuneiform. [[excavation-10|Excavations]] at the ancient city of Uruk have uncovered thousands of such records, most of which list food rations, taxes and [[property-10|property]].

At first, writing served a purely economic [[function-10|function]]. Records of land ownership acted as early [[deed-10|deeds]], proving a family's right to its fields. Gradually, however, the system was [[adopt-10|adopted]] for many other purposes, and within a few centuries it could [[encompass-10|encompass a range of]] texts, including laws, letters, prayers and literature. The Epic of Gilgamesh, which draws heavily on Mesopotamian [[mythology-10|mythology]], is among the oldest written stories in the world. In Egypt, meanwhile, hieroglyphs were [[carve-10|carved into]] the stone walls of temples and tombs, and many historians [[attribute-10|attribute]] their development to a separate local tradition rather than to foreign influence.

Because early scripts contained hundreds of signs, [[literacy-10|literacy]] was limited to a small group. Scribes spent years in [[specialized-10|specialized]] schools learning their craft, and they occupied a respected place in the [[structure-10|social structure]]. Rulers, too, used writing to impress their subjects, and royal victories were [[inscribe-10|inscribed in stone]] for all to see. Only in the first millennium BCE, when the Phoenicians spread a simple alphabet, did reading and writing become accessible to a much wider population.

title: Stories in Motion: The Hula of Hawaii
paragraphs: To many visitors, the hula is simply a pleasant show for tourists, featuring grass skirts and [[sway-11|swaying hips]]. This popular [[image-11|image]], however, is a [[stereotype-11|stereotype]] that hides a much deeper meaning. For Native Hawaiians, the hula is a living [[tradition-11|tradition]] that preserves history, family lines and religious belief in a culture that, for centuries, had no written language.

The exact origins of the dance are uncertain, but oral histories and archaeological [[evidence-11|evidence suggest]] that it developed over many centuries after Polynesian voyagers settled the islands. Traditionally, dancing was a sacred [[ritual-11|ritual]]. Before performing, students placed offerings [[altar-11|on the altar]] of Laka, the goddess of the hula, often decorating it with plants gathered from the forest. Performances were [[accompany-11|accompanied by]] chanting and by the rhythm of drums made from gourds.

Every movement carries a specific meaning. A [[graceful-11|graceful]] motion of the hands might represent falling rain or waves rolling onto the shore, while dancers who [[sway-11|sway gently]] from side to side can [[evoke-11|evoke an image]] of palm trees in the wind. Some older forms are [[energetic-11|highly energetic]] and powerful, whereas others are slow and soft. Performers often wear [[elaborate-11|elaborate costumes]], including the lei, [[garland-11|a garland of flowers]] or leaves, together with [[floral-11|floral decorations]] around the head, wrists and ankles.

In the nineteenth century, the hula came under severe pressure. Christian missionaries, who arrived in 1820, gained a [[influence-11|strong influence over]] the ruling family and [[discourage-11|strongly discouraged]] public performances, which they considered improper. As a result, the dance was practised largely in secret for several decades. Its fortunes changed during [[reign-11|the reign of]] King David Kalākaua, who ruled from 1874 to 1891. He worked hard to [[revive-11|revive]] traditional arts and famously described the hula as the heartbeat of the Hawaiian people.

Today the hula is enjoying a remarkable comeback. The Merrie Monarch Festival, held every spring in the town of Hilo and named after Kalākaua himself, is a week-long [[celebration-11|celebration]] that attracts dancers from across the islands and beyond. Supporters point to [[benefit-11|the benefits of]] the practice: it helps keep the Hawaiian language alive, connects young people with their ancestors and provides excellent physical exercise. Above all, it reminds audiences that a dance can be a history book written in movement.

title: The Power of Silence: The Art of Mime
paragraphs: Mime is the art of telling a story without words. Using only the body, the face and carefully chosen [[gesture-12|gestures]], a performer can [[portray-12|portray a character]], express strong feelings and even build entire imaginary worlds. Although it may look simple, mime demands years of training, and its history stretches back [[considerably-12|considerably]] further than most people realise.

The form [[emerge-12|emerged]] in ancient Greece and Rome, where performers entertained crowds with [[humorous-12|humorous]] scenes from daily life. Centuries later, the travelling companies of Italian commedia dell'arte [[merge-12|merged]] spoken comedy with physical tricks, relying on masks and [[exaggerated-12|exaggerated movements]] to make their characters instantly recognisable. In nineteenth-century Paris, Jean-Gaspard Deburau became [[renowned-12|renowned for]] his sad, white-faced Pierrot, a figure that audiences found both comic and deeply moving.

In the twentieth century, Étienne Decroux developed a strict system of physical training, and his student Marcel Marceau went on to become the most [[prominent-12|prominent]] mime artist in the world. Marceau's character Bip, with his striped shirt and battered hat, appeared in countless short pieces. Some were light-hearted, while others explored [[frailty-12|human frailty]], loneliness and the [[conflict-12|inner conflict]] between hope and fear. One celebrated sketch follows an entire human life in just a few minutes, [[culminate-12|culminating in]] the quiet moment of death.

One of the most important skills a mime artist possesses is the ability to [[illusion-12|create an illusion]]. By pressing flat hands against empty air, a performer can make an audience believe in an invisible wall; by leaning forward at a steep angle, they suggest a powerful wind. Traditionally, mime artists avoid real [[prop-12|props]], so every object must be imagined. To achieve this, they must [[sharpen-12|sharpen]] their powers of observation, studying exactly how people lift a heavy suitcase or climb a ladder.

Not every performance is realistic, however. Some pieces move beyond [[literal-12|literal]] actions to explore [[abstract-12|abstract ideas]] such as time, freedom or memory. A skilled performer can also use stillness to [[atmosphere-12|create a tense atmosphere]], holding the attention of a whole theatre without a single sound. Such scenes are often [[reminiscent-12|reminiscent of]] silent films, and it is no coincidence that stars like Charlie Chaplin relied on similar techniques. Today, drama schools use mime [[effectively-12|effectively]] to teach body awareness, proving that this ancient art still has much to say without speaking a word.

title: The Global Journey of Nurses
paragraphs: Every year, tens of thousands of nurses leave their home countries to [[abroad-13|work abroad]]. [[decade-13|Over the past decade]], this movement has grown into a [[complex-13|highly complex]] global system that links hospitals in wealthy nations with training colleges in poorer ones. [[estimate-13|It is estimated that]] one in eight nurses worldwide now practises outside the country where they were born or trained, and the figure continues to rise.

The [[primary-13|primary cause]] of this flow is a [[shortage-13|severe shortage]] of [[qualified-13|qualified staff]] in high-income countries. Populations there are ageing, and [[bulk-13|the bulk of the work]] in hospitals and care homes falls on nurses. At the same time, many young people choose other careers, so the [[supply-13|supply]] of new graduates cannot keep pace with demand. When a hospital cannot [[vacancy-13|fill a vacancy]], managers often recruit overseas, and many nurses are [[lure-13|lured by high salaries]], modern equipment and the chance for their children to [[abroad-13|study abroad]].

For the countries that lose these workers, the consequences can be serious. In parts of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, a single hospital may depend on a handful of nurses to [[administer-13|administer treatment]] to hundreds of patients. When even a few leave, the result can be a [[cripple-13|crippling shortage]] that leaves rural clinics staffed by assistants with only [[rudimentary-13|rudimentary skills]]. During the [[epidemic-13|outbreak of an epidemic]] such as cholera, the loss is felt most sharply, because there are too few trained hands to [[administer-13|administer a vaccine]] or isolate the sick, and disease can [[rampant-13|run rampant]].

[[standpoint-13|From an economic standpoint]], the picture is mixed. Nurses who [[abroad-13|live abroad]] often send money home, and these payments support families and local businesses. However, governments that paid to educate them receive little direct return on that investment, and health systems in countries [[cripple-13|crippled by debt]] find it almost impossible to compete on pay. Critics argue that foreign recruitment speeds up the [[decline-13|steady decline]] of public health services that were already fragile.

Several strategies have been proposed to [[stem-13|stem the flow]]. The World Health Organization publishes a list of countries from which active recruitment is discouraged, although its code is voluntary. Some sending nations have raised wages or offered housing in order to [[retain-13|retain staff]], while others have signed agreements under which receiving countries fund extra training places. A few governments even encourage temporary migration, hoping that nurses will return [[decade-13|within a decade]] with valuable new experience.

Ultimately, the migration of nurses is a [[complex-13|complex issue]] with no simple solution. Individuals have a right to seek a better life, yet whole communities may suffer when their carers leave. Balancing these interests will remain a [[primary-13|primary concern]] for health planners for many years to come.

title: Running for the Mind
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, exercise was valued mainly for its effects on the heart and muscles. It was [[previously-14|previously thought]] that the adult brain could not grow new cells and that our [[capacity-14|capacity for learning]] simply shrank with age. Over the last thirty years, however, a growing body of evidence has challenged that view, and scientists now believe there is a [[link-14|strong link between]] physical activity and mental health.

Much of the early evidence came from [[rodent-14|rodent studies]]. In a well-known series of experiments, mice that had access to a running wheel produced more new neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory, than mice that remained inactive. The runners also performed better in water mazes, which test [[spatial-14|spatial memory]]. These findings suggested that [[aerobic-14|aerobic exercise]] could [[stimulate-14|stimulate the brain]] by increasing blood flow and releasing chemicals that support the growth of nerve cells.

Human studies soon followed. [[indicate-14|Research indicates]] that older adults who walk briskly for forty minutes three times a week show improvements in [[cognition-14|cognition and memory]] within a year. Brain scans of such volunteers reveal that the hippocampus can actually increase in size, reversing the [[deterioration-14|gradual deterioration]] normally seen in later life. Regular activity also appears to [[counteract-14|counteract the effects]] of stress hormones, which may explain why people who exercise often report better [[concentration-14|concentration]] at work.

The implications are significant, especially in view of the [[gravity-14|gravity of the situation]] facing ageing societies. Every year millions of people are [[diagnose-14|diagnosed with]] [[dementia-14|dementia]], a [[disorder-14|disorder]] for which there is still no cure. Although exercise cannot guarantee protection, large population studies suggest that people who remain physically active have a noticeably lower [[dementia-14|risk of dementia]]. Moreover, in patients who already have [[impaired-14|impaired memory]], regular movement may help to [[stave-off-14|stave off decline]] for several years.

The benefits are not limited to the elderly. [[aerobic-14|Aerobic activity]] helps the body [[regulate-14|regulate emotions]] and can [[mood-14|improve mood]], and doctors increasingly recommend it alongside medication for patients with depression or a [[disorder-14|sleep disorder]]. Children who take part in daily physical education often pay more attention in class and find it easier to complete their homework.

Nevertheless, researchers remain cautious. Many studies are small, and it is difficult to separate the effects of exercise from those of diet, education and social contact. It is also unclear exactly how much activity is needed, or which type is most effective. Even so, the message from the laboratory is encouraging: a brisk walk may do as much for the mind as it does for the body.

title: From Laboratory to Pharmacy
paragraphs: Bringing a new medicine to market is one of the longest and most expensive processes in modern science. It can take more than ten years and cost over a billion dollars, and only [[fraction-15|a tiny fraction]] of the compounds that researchers examine will ever reach patients. Each stage of the [[investigation-15|scientific investigation]] is designed to answer one central question: is the drug both safe and effective?

The journey usually begins with a [[theoretical-15|theoretical model]]. Scientists study how a disease works at the molecular level and identify a protein or process that a drug could [[target-15|specifically target]]. Using computers, they then screen thousands of chemical structures to find a [[substance-15|substance]] with [[desirable-15|desirable qualities]], such as stability and the ability to reach the right part of the body. Promising candidates are tested on a [[culture-15|cell culture]] grown in the laboratory, which allows researchers to observe whether a compound can [[combat-15|combat disease]] without harming healthy tissue.

Compounds that pass these early checks move on to animal studies. Here the aim is to [[ascertain-15|ascertain whether]] the drug is [[toxic-15|toxic]], how quickly the body can [[absorb-15|absorb]] it, and how long it remains in the blood. Any compound that produces [[toxic-15|toxic effects]] at low doses is [[deem-15|deemed unsafe]] and abandoned. Researchers also experiment with different forms of the medicine, since coatings and additives can [[enhance-15|enhance the effect]] of the active compound or ensure it is [[absorb-15|easily absorbed]] in the stomach.

Only then does testing in humans begin. Clinical trials normally take place in three phases. In the first, a small group of healthy volunteers receives the drug, and doctors [[monitor-15|closely monitor]] their heart rate, blood pressure and other signs [[interval-15|at regular intervals]]. The second phase involves several hundred patients and examines whether the treatment can actually [[alleviate-15|alleviate symptoms]]. The third phase may include thousands of people in many countries and compares the new drug with existing treatments or with a placebo, a harmless pill that looks identical. Usually neither the patients nor the doctors know who receives which, so that their expectations cannot affect the [[outcome-15|final outcome]].

Trials for [[chronic-15|chronic conditions]] such as arthritis or diabetes often last for years, because researchers need to know whether the benefits continue and whether symptoms [[recur-15|recur]] once treatment stops. If the results are positive, the company applies to a regulatory authority for approval.

Even after approval, the work is not finished. Once a company begins to [[manufacture-15|manufacture]] the drug on a large scale, regulators continue to collect reports of side effects, since rare problems may appear only when millions of people use it. In this sense, the study of a medicine never truly ends.

title: Walking to Machu Picchu
paragraphs: High in the Andes of southern Peru lies Machu Picchu, a fifteenth-century stone city that has become one of the most famous [[site-16|archaeological sites]] in the world. Built on a narrow ridge between two mountains, it is widely regarded as an [[marvel-16|engineering marvel]], and its [[spectacular-16|spectacular views]] [[draw-16|draw visitors]] from every continent. Although a train and bus now make the city [[accessible-16|accessible]] to most tourists, many [[adventurous-16|adventurous travellers]] prefer to arrive the traditional way: on foot, along the Inca Trail.

The trail is part of an [[network-16|extensive network]] of paths that the Incas [[construct-16|constructed]] across their empire, linking cities, farms and fortresses over thousands of kilometres. The classic route covers around 43 kilometres and usually takes four days. Hikers climb steep stone staircases, cross a pass more than 4,200 metres above sea level, and walk through cloud forest full of orchids and [[native-16|native species]] of birds. Along the way they pass several smaller ruins, some of which appear to have served [[ceremonial-16|ceremonial purposes]].

Machu Picchu itself has long [[imagination-16|captured the imagination]] of scholars. [[archeologist-16|Archeologists believe]] it was a royal estate rather than an ordinary town, but [[precisely-16|precisely]] why it was abandoned after less than a century is still an [[mystery-16|unsolved mystery]]. Because Spanish conquerors never found the place, its buildings are unusually [[preserve-16|well preserved]], offering researchers valuable information [[pertain-16|pertaining to]] Inca religion, astronomy and daily life.

Its popularity, however, has created problems. By the end of the twentieth century, erosion and litter were damaging the trail, so the Peruvian government decided to [[institute-16|institute a system]] of permits. Today [[restriction-16|strict restrictions]] limit the number of people on the trail to about 500 per day, including guides and porters, and every hiker must travel with a licensed tour company. The trail is also closed each February for maintenance.

These rules mean that permits often sell out months in advance, which frustrates some visitors. [[upside-16|The upside is]] that the path is far less crowded than before. Moreover, the porters, most of whom are [[native-16|native to]] the region, now benefit from fairer wages and legal limits on the weight of the loads they carry.

Walking the trail offers none of the comforts of a [[luxury-16|luxury hotel]]. Nights are spent in tents, temperatures can fall below freezing, and the high altitude often causes headaches and breathlessness. Yet for most hikers, the moment they pass through the Sun Gate at dawn and see the ancient city below makes every difficult step worthwhile.

title: Travelling Lightly
paragraphs: Tourism is one of the largest industries on the planet, and its environmental costs are considerable. Crowded beaches, polluted rivers and damaged coral reefs are familiar sights in many a [[destination-17|popular destination]]. In response, a growing number of travellers and businesses have embraced [[concept-17|the concept of]] ecotourism, a form of travel that aims to protect nature rather than exploit it.

Although definitions vary, most experts agree on several [[principle-17|basic principles]]. Ecotourism should take place in natural areas, reduce its impact on the environment, educate visitors, and bring real benefits to local communities. Trips that meet these standards may take guests into [[remote-17|remote areas]] of rainforest or into an [[wilderness-17|untouched wilderness]], but the goal is never simply to travel [[pleasure-17|for pleasure]]. Instead, visitors are encouraged to understand the [[delicate-17|delicate ecosystem]] around them and the people who depend on it.

[[practice-17|In practice]], responsible operators [[strive-17|strive to]] limit harm in many ways. Their [[accommodations-17|accommodations]] are often small lodges built from local materials and powered by solar energy. Water is reused, a [[recycling-17|recycling scheme]] handles rubbish, and guests are asked to [[avoid-17|avoid contact]] with wild animals, which can be frightened or even [[injure-17|injured]] by careless visitors. Many projects also rely on a [[volunteer-17|team of volunteers]] who plant trees, count wildlife or teach English in nearby villages. Local guides help visitors overcome the [[barrier-17|language barrier]] and explain traditions that outsiders might otherwise misunderstand.

However, not every trip marketed as 'eco' deserves the label. Because the term attracts positive [[publicity-17|publicity]], some companies use it simply to sell ordinary holidays at higher prices, a [[practice-17|common practice]] known as greenwashing. In such cases, hotels may still [[dump-17|dump waste]] into rivers or build roads through protected forests. Critics also point out that the long-haul flight needed to reach a distant jungle is often [[culprit-17|the main culprit]] behind a trip's carbon footprint, regardless of how green the lodge may be.

For this reason, travellers are advised to remain [[wary-17|wary of]] vague claims. Genuine operators are usually certified by an independent body and can explain exactly where their profits go. Some researchers suggest placing each trip in a [[category-17|separate category]] according to how strictly it meets agreed standards, so that consumers can compare offers more easily.

Despite its weaknesses, ecotourism has achieved real successes. In Costa Rica and parts of East Africa, income from visitors has persuaded communities to protect forests and wildlife instead of cutting down trees or hunting animals. When it is done well, travel can be both a source of enjoyment and a genuine force for conservation.

title: Holidays That Teach
paragraphs: For many people, a holiday means lying on the sand at a [[resort-18|seaside resort]] with nothing more demanding to do than choose a drink. Yet a growing number of travellers want more from their time off. Learning vacations, in which participants combine travel with study, have become one of the fastest-growing sectors of the tourism industry. [[survey-18|According to a survey]] carried out by one travel association, almost a third of adults would consider a holiday built around a new skill.

The range of options is remarkably [[broad-18|broad]]. Visitors can [[enroll-18|enroll in a course]] in Italian at a language school in Florence, study photography in Iceland, or learn to paint among the [[colorful-18|colorful markets]] of Morocco. Food-based trips are especially popular: participants visit farms to buy [[ingredient-18|fresh ingredients]] and then spend the afternoon learning to prepare the [[cuisine-18|local cuisine]] under the guidance of a professional chef. Others join research projects, helping scientists record whales or excavate ancient settlements, and thus contribute to a real [[endeavor-18|scientific endeavor]].

Such trips appeal to people who wish to [[acquire-18|acquire skills]] while enjoying new surroundings. Many courses are [[residential-18|residential]], meaning that students live together in a shared house or hotel, which allows them to practise constantly and [[hone-18|hone their skills]] outside formal lessons. The [[content-18|course content]] is usually practical rather than academic, and most programmes are designed so that beginners find the first steps [[breeze-18|a breeze]]. More demanding activities, such as diving or mountaineering, take place under [[supervision-18|close supervision]] by experienced instructors.

Cost is an important consideration. Some specialist programmes, particularly those with expert tutors and very small groups, can be [[costly-18|extremely costly]]. However, travellers [[budget-18|on a budget]] have alternatives. Language schools in Latin America, for example, often arrange homestays with local families, which are far more [[economical-18|economical]] than hotels and also give students [[taste-18|a taste of local life]]. Some educational trips for teenagers are partly paid for by a [[sponsor-18|corporate sponsor]], such as a bank or a technology firm, which reduces the fee for each participant.

Supporters argue that learning holidays offer benefits that last long after the suitcase has been unpacked. Learning is an [[ongoing-18|ongoing process]], and a week spent mastering a new technique can inspire people to continue studying at home. Participants also tend to form deeper connections with the places they visit, because they interact with local people rather than simply observing them from a tour bus.

Critics, on the other hand, warn that some programmes provide little real teaching and are merely ordinary holidays with a fashionable label. Choosing the wrong course can be a [[costly-18|costly mistake]], so experts recommend reading reviews and checking the teachers' experience carefully before booking.

title: Surviving the First Five Years
paragraphs: Every year, thousands of people open their own shops, cafés and online stores, yet a large proportion of these ventures fail to [[afloat-19|stay afloat]] beyond their fifth year. Researchers who study small enterprises have tried to identify the [[characteristic-19|common characteristics]] of those that survive. Although no single formula guarantees success, several factors appear again and again.

The first is careful planning before a business opens. The [[initial-19|initial costs]] of renting premises, buying equipment and hiring staff are often higher than owners expect, and when sales grow more slowly than [[project-19|projected]], cash quickly runs out. Owners who base their plans on realistic [[project-19|projected figures]] and seek [[sound-19|sound advice]] from accountants are far less likely to face [[financial-19|financial difficulties]] in the first year. Banks and other lenders also pay [[particular-19|particular attention]] to such plans when deciding whether to offer a loan, and a plan that shows a clear route to [[profit-19|making a profit]] reassures [[potential-19|potential investors]] as well.

The second factor concerns what the business actually sells. A small company is usually [[compete-19|unable to compete]] with large chains on price alone, because those chains buy in huge quantities. Instead, successful owners tend to [[niche-19|carve out a niche]]: they offer a [[product-19|product]] or service that big retailers overlook, such as handmade furniture or food for people with [[particular-19|particular]] dietary needs. Having a [[unique-19|unique selling point]] gives them [[edge-19|a competitive edge]], since customers who want something specific are often willing to pay more for it.

Customer relationships form the third element. Independent businesses can offer [[personalized-19|personalized service]] in a way that large firms rarely manage: a bookseller who remembers a regular customer's tastes, or a bakery that designs cakes for individual events. Over time, this attention helps owners [[reputation-19|build a reputation]] that spreads by word of mouth, which is [[vital-19|vital for success]] when there is little money for advertising. Equally important is the [[motivation-19|motivation]] of the owner and staff. In a small team, a [[motivation-19|lack of motivation]] in even one person is quickly noticed by customers.

Finally, experts stress that setbacks are normal. Changes in the wider economy [[inevitably-19|will inevitably affect]] small firms, which have fewer savings to fall back on than their larger rivals. A useful [[tip-19|tip]] offered by many business advisers is to keep a cash reserve covering at least three months of expenses. Such [[sound-19|sound financial management]] does not remove risk entirely, but it allows a business to survive a difficult season and continue to [[compete-19|compete for customers]] once conditions improve.

title: Why We Stay Faithful to Brands
paragraphs: Walk into any supermarket and you will see shoppers reaching for the same [[brand-20|brand]] of coffee or washing powder week after week, often without even looking at alternatives. This [[phenomenon-20|phenomenon]], known as [[loyalty-20|brand loyalty]], has fascinated marketers for decades. Why do people remain attached to one name when cheaper or better products sit on the same shelf?

Part of the answer lies in the [[bond-20|emotional bond]] that forms between consumers and the companies they buy from. When a product [[consistently-20|consistently delivers]] the same quality, customers learn to trust it, and it gradually [[staple-20|becomes a staple]] of their weekly shopping. Researchers have found that once this trust is established, many buyers [[ignore-20|completely ignore]] competing offers, even when these are heavily discounted. For some goods, such as trainers, watches or handbags, attachment is also linked to [[status-20|social status]]: owning a particular label signals wealth or taste to others.

Companies spend enormous sums trying to [[convince-20|convince consumers]] that their goods deserve this kind of devotion. A [[conglomerate-20|multinational conglomerate]] may own dozens of labels and [[promote-20|actively promote]] each one with a different personality. [[endorsement-20|Celebrity endorsement]] remains a popular strategy, particularly among younger buyers with a [[thirst-20|thirst for]] novelty and glamour. However, the popularity created by a famous face can be [[fleeting-20|fleeting]]; if the star falls out of favour, sales may fall too.

The situation is further complicated by a [[burgeoning-20|burgeoning middle class]] in many developing economies. These new consumers are often [[selective-20|highly selective]], comparing prices and reviews online before making a purchase. For them, a [[passion-20|passion for]] one company is less common than a practical interest in value. As a result, some analysts argue that traditional [[loyalty-20|loyalty]] is declining, and that firms will need new methods to [[reverse-20|reverse the trend]].

Yet the evidence suggests that [[loyalty-20|customer loyalty]] is far from dead. Studies show that businesses with strong customer relationships [[outperform-20|consistently outperform]] their rivals over the long term, because keeping an existing customer costs much less than attracting a new one. Many companies now reward regular buyers through apps and points schemes, hoping to turn occasional shoppers into devoted fans. In the end, most experts believe the view that will [[prevail-20|prevail]] is a simple one: people stay faithful to [[brand-20|brands]] that treat them well and keep their promises.

title: The Outsourcing Debate
paragraphs: Over the past four decades, a [[shift-21|major shift]] has taken place in the way companies organise their work. Instead of employing every worker in their home country, many businesses now send tasks such as customer service, software development and accounting to other parts of the world. This practice, known as outsourcing, has become one of the most discussed features of the global economy and remains a [[controversy-21|subject of controversy]].

The growth of outsourcing happened to [[coincide-21|coincide with]] two important developments: the spread of cheap, fast internet connections and the opening of large economies such as India and China to foreign investment. For a [[firm-21|firm]] based in a [[wealthy-21|wealthy nation]], the prospect of paying far lower wages overseas was highly [[enticing-21|enticing]]. Cities like Bangalore quickly became [[epicenter-21|the epicenter of]] the new industry, and international companies [[branch-21|opened branches]] there employing thousands of graduates.

[[proponent-21|Proponents argue that]] outsourcing has been [[boon-21|a real boon]] for both sides. Companies reduce costs and can offer services around the clock, while developing countries gain jobs, skills and investment that help them [[catch-up-21|catch up with]] richer economies. Supporters also [[point-21|make the point]] that cost is rarely the only reason for moving work abroad; access to talented engineers is often a [[decisive-21|decisive factor]].

[[opponent-21|Opponents of]] outsourcing, however, focus on the workers left behind. When a company closes a call centre at home, whole towns may be [[confront-21|confronted with]] unemployment, and [[remainder-21|the remainder of]] the staff often fear that their own jobs will be next. Critics also note that overseas centres suffer from [[turnover-21|high staff turnover]], as employees who [[routinely-21|routinely work overtime]] through the night soon leave for better-paid positions. Recruiting and training their replacements adds hidden costs.

Recent surveys of business leaders suggest that [[preponderance-21|the preponderance of opinion]] still favours outsourcing, at least for large companies. Nevertheless, with a [[looming-21|looming]] shortage of skilled workers and rising wages in traditional outsourcing centres, many businesses are reconsidering their strategy. Some have brought certain operations back home, while others spread work across several countries to reduce risk. Whatever they decide, managers will have to [[confront-21|confront the issue]] of how to balance efficiency with responsibility to their own communities.

title: Connected Lives
paragraphs: In the early 2000s, only a small number of people used websites to share news with friends. Within a decade, however, social networking had [[explode-22|exploded in popularity]], and today billions of users [[post-22|post]] photos, comments and updates every day. According to the latest [[statistics-22|statistics]], the average user spends more than two hours a day on such platforms. This [[trend-22|growing trend]] has transformed the way people [[interact-22|interact with]] one another.

For many, the benefits are obvious. Social networks allow users to [[contact-22|keep in contact]] with relatives abroad, reconnect with an [[acquaintance-22|old acquaintance]] from school, or join an [[community-22|online community]] of people who share an unusual hobby. They also encourage [[exchange-22|the exchange of ideas]] across borders. Job seekers use professional sites to build networks and to [[pursue-22|pursue a career]] in fields that might otherwise be difficult to enter. For small organisations, the [[immense-22|immense]] reach of these platforms offers publicity at almost no cost.

Yet researchers who [[carry-out-22|carry out studies]] on social media warn of [[consequence-22|negative consequences]]. Young [[adolescent-22|adolescents]] are thought to be [[susceptible-22|particularly susceptible to]] the stress of comparing themselves with others, since their sense of identity is still forming. Content that is [[apparently-22|apparently harmless]], such as carefully edited holiday photos, may leave teenagers feeling that their own lives are dull. Some psychologists also believe that heavy use reduces [[contact-22|face-to-face contact]], although the evidence on this question is mixed.

Governments have responded in different ways. Several countries have chosen to [[impose-22|impose restrictions]] on how platforms collect personal data, and some have proposed banning accounts for children under a certain age. Campaigners hope such rules will help to [[eradicate-22|eradicate]] online bullying, though most experts doubt that any law can remove it completely. Meanwhile, the companies themselves have [[undergo-22|undergone changes]], introducing tools that allow users to limit their screen time or hide harmful material.

It is still too early to judge the long-term effects of this technology. The story of social networking continues to [[unfold-22|unfold]], and each new platform brings fresh opportunities as well as fresh concerns. What seems certain is that online networks will remain a central part of social life, and that learning to use them wisely is now an essential skill for people of all ages.

title: The Leaking Pipeline
paragraphs: Over the past fifty years, considerable [[progress-23|progress]] has been made towards [[equality-23|gender equality]] in education. In many countries, women now earn [[approximately-23|approximately half]] of all science degrees, and their [[academic-23|academic performance]] at university often matches or exceeds that of men. Yet the number of women decreases sharply at each stage of a research career. Scientists call this pattern the 'leaking pipeline', and the question of why it [[persist-23|persists]] has become a major focus of study.

One explanation concerns money and working conditions. Early-career researchers usually depend on short-term contracts, and competition for [[funding-23|funding for research]] is intense. Several studies have found [[discrepancy-23|a significant discrepancy between]] the grants awarded to male and female applicants, even when their records are similar. Many women also report that their salaries are not [[commensurate-23|commensurate with]] their experience. Faced with such conditions, some decide that the effort is simply not worth the reward.

Family responsibilities form a second factor. In many societies, women still [[bear-23|bear the burden]] of most childcare, and the years when a scientist must publish widely are often the same years when people start families. A career break can have [[dire-23|dire consequences]]: [[absence-23|a long absence]] from the laboratory may mean falling behind in a fast-moving field. Parents who return frequently [[struggle-23|struggle to cope]] with long hours, and many describe [[frustration-23|growing frustration]] at workplaces that expect staff to [[devote-23|devote]] evenings and weekends to their experiments.

Workplace culture also plays a role. Female researchers describe being asked to spend [[inordinate-23|an inordinate amount of]] time on committee work and teaching, tasks that rarely lead to promotion. Others mention constant [[pressure-23|pressure]] to prove that they deserve their positions. [[absence-23|In the absence of]] role models, young women may find it hard to imagine a future for themselves in senior posts.

Many universities are now trying to address these problems. One of the most effective measures appears to be the introduction of [[mentor-23|mentor programs]]. [[mentor-23|A trusted mentor]] can [[guidance-23|provide guidance]] on career choices, share [[invaluable-23|invaluable advice]] about grant applications, and help younger colleagues build professional networks. Just as importantly, experienced colleagues can [[validate-23|validate]] the experiences of women who feel isolated, reassuring them that their difficulties are not a sign of personal failure. Such schemes, combined with fairer [[funding-23|funding]] systems and flexible working, may finally help to close the leak.

title: Designing Cities for Everyone
paragraphs: For people who use wheelchairs, an ordinary trip to the shops can involve a series of obstacles. The World Health Organization estimates that more than a billion people worldwide live with some form of [[disability-24|disability]], and wheelchair users [[account-for-24|account for]] a significant share of this group. Yet many buildings and public spaces are still designed as if everyone were [[capable-24|physically capable]] of climbing stairs.

The problems begin outdoors. [[curb-24|A high curb]] without a lowered section can make it impossible to cross a street, and pavements with [[slope-24|a steep slope]] are both tiring and dangerous. Tiles that become [[slippery-24|slippery when wet]] cause wheels to lose their grip, while [[terrain-24|uneven terrain]] in parks and older town centres limits access to [[recreation-24|outdoor recreation]]. Even where [[ramp-24|a wheelchair ramp]] has been installed, it is sometimes too steep to use safely without help.

Inside buildings, the difficulties continue. Narrow doorways and [[corridor-24|narrow corridors]] can prevent a wheelchair from turning, and [[interior-24|interior doors]] are often too heavy to open from a seated position. [[switch-24|A light switch]] placed high on the wall may be out of reach, and older lifts, where they exist at all, are frequently too small. Adapting such buildings can [[necessitate-24|necessitate changes]] to their basic structure, which is one reason why owners delay the work.

Cost is a serious issue for wheelchair users themselves as well. Many [[disability-24|people with disabilities]] [[poverty-24|live in poverty]] and cannot afford the latest equipment. Traditional wheelchairs can be heavy and [[unwieldy-24|unwieldy]], especially in crowded places, whereas modern models with [[compact-24|a compact design]] are lighter and easier to fold but considerably more expensive. For someone who is [[incapacitated-24|temporarily incapacitated]] after an accident, even renting a suitable chair can be a financial strain.

Fortunately, examples of good practice [[abound-24|abound]]. Many cities now [[update-24|regularly update]] their building regulations, requiring [[exterior-24|exterior doors]] to open automatically and new pavements to include gentle [[ramp-24|ramps]] at crossings. Designers point out that such features help not only wheelchair users but also parents with pushchairs, elderly people and travellers with heavy luggage. When accessibility is considered from the very start of a project, rather than added later, a city becomes easier for everyone to move through.

title: Do We Really Learn in Different Ways?
paragraphs: Walk into any [[conventional-25|conventional classroom]] and you will probably see a teacher speaking at the front while rows of students listen and take notes. For much of the twentieth century, this [[approach-25|approach]] was rarely questioned. Yet teachers have long noticed that pupils respond very differently to the same lesson. Some remember every word they hear, others need to see information laid out on a page, and a few seem unable to sit still. Such observations gave rise to the popular theory of learning styles, which claims that each person has a [[dominant-25|dominant learning style]].

The best-known version of the theory divides learners into three groups. [[auditory-25|Auditory learners]] are said to absorb spoken information easily; they may [[recite-25|recite poems from memory]] after hearing them only a few times, and they often have strong [[verbal-25|verbal skills]]. Visual learners, by contrast, prefer to [[diagram-25|draw a diagram]] or study a chart, and they pay close attention to a speaker's [[facial-25|facial expressions]] and gestures. Finally, [[kinesthetic-25|kinesthetic learners]] understand ideas best when they can [[manipulate-25|manipulate objects]], build models or move around the room.

Supporters argue that recognising these differences can transform a child's experience of school. A pupil who is forced to listen to long lectures may begin to [[fidget-25|fidget in their seat]], and teachers sometimes mistake this restlessness for bad behaviour. If the problem is ignored, it can seriously [[hinder-25|hinder learning]] and cause the student to [[confidence-25|lose confidence]]. In such [[circumstance-25|circumstances]], small changes, such as allowing short breaks for movement or offering hands-on tasks, can remove an important [[obstruction-25|obstruction to progress]].

However, many researchers remain sceptical. Several large studies have found little evidence that teaching students in their preferred style improves test results. Critics also point out that labelling a child as a particular type of learner may limit them. A student who believes he is purely a "listener" might avoid reading, while one who describes herself as a [[solitary-25|solitary learner]] may miss the benefits of group discussion. In the critics' view, the theory has become [[conventional-25|conventional wisdom]] without ever being properly tested.

Most experts now recommend a middle path. Rather than sorting pupils into boxes, teachers can [[incorporate-25|incorporate]] a [[blend-25|blend of]] activities into every lesson, combining spoken explanation, images and practical work. This makes it more likely that all students will be [[expose-25|exposed to]] ideas in several forms, which appears to strengthen memory. Just as importantly, pupils need [[encouragement-25|constant encouragement]] to try methods that do not come naturally to them. A varied, [[approach-25|practical approach]] of this kind may not match the neat categories of the original theory, but it reflects what good teachers have always known: people learn best when lessons engage the mind in more than one way.

title: Learning at the Kitchen Table: The Rise of Home Education
paragraphs: In most countries, [[compulsory-26|compulsory education]] means that children must receive schooling until a certain age. However, the law does not always say that this schooling has to take place in a school building. In many places, parents may legally teach their children at home, and in recent decades this option has moved from the edges of society towards the mainstream. Although home-educated children remain a [[relatively-26|relatively small]] group, their numbers have grown steadily, and the practice is now far more [[widespread-26|widespread]] than it was a generation ago.

Families choose home education for many reasons. Some parents are [[dissatisfied-26|dissatisfied with]] local schools, pointing to overcrowded classes or low standards. Others are [[concerned-26|deeply concerned]] about bullying, or they feel that schools cannot [[address-26|address the needs of]] children with [[exceptional-26|exceptional talent]] or with learning difficulties. For another group, the decision reflects a personal [[philosophy-26|philosophy of education]]: they believe that children learn most effectively when they follow their own interests rather than a fixed timetable.

The way home [[instruction-26|instruction]] is organised varies enormously. Some families recreate the school day at the kitchen table, using textbooks and set lessons. Others prefer a [[novel-26|novel approach]] in which learning happens through projects, museum visits and everyday activities. Parents who lack [[prior-26|prior experience]] of teaching, or who feel less confident in subjects such as advanced mathematics, often [[tutor-26|hire a tutor]] or join cooperative groups where several families share the teaching. Online courses now offer a [[vast-26|vast range of]] materials, which has made home education far easier than before.

Governments have responded in different ways. In some countries, school attendance is [[obligatory-26|legally obligatory]], and home education is permitted only in [[exceptional-26|exceptional circumstances]], such as serious illness. Elsewhere, it is allowed but closely monitored. Authorities may [[mandate-26|mandate]] [[periodic-26|periodic assessments]], require parents to submit learning plans, or demand [[prior-26|prior approval]] before a child is withdrawn from school. Supporters of home education argue that such rules are unnecessary, while critics insist that without them, the state cannot be sure that every child is being [[adequately-26|adequately]] taught.

The debate often centres on two questions: academic results and social development. On the former, research suggests that the [[vast-26|vast]] [[majority-26|majority]] of home-educated students perform at least as well as their schooled classmates, although these studies are often based on families who volunteer to take part. On the [[latter-26|latter]], opinions are more divided. Critics worry that children may miss the daily contact with other young people that schools provide, whereas supporters reply that sports clubs and community activities offer plenty of social opportunities. Home education is unlikely to replace schools, but for some families it has become a genuine [[alternative-26|alternative to]] the classroom.

title: Meeting the Needs of Gifted Children
paragraphs: For many years, schools focused their extra resources on pupils who were struggling. [[remedial-27|Remedial classes]] in reading and mathematics were common, while children who were far ahead of their classmates were expected to look after themselves. Today, educators increasingly [[recognize-27|recognize the need for]] specialised support at the other end of the ability range as well. [[gifted-27|Gifted children]], it is argued, have needs that are just as real as those of pupils who fall behind.

Defining high ability, however, is not simple. Different countries and researchers offer a [[interpretation-27|different interpretation]] of the term. Some rely mainly on intelligence tests, while others look for [[extraordinary-27|extraordinary talent]] in music, art or sport. Most experts agree that ability exists on a scale: a [[moderately-27|moderately]] [[gifted-27|gifted]] child may simply learn faster than average, whereas a [[profoundly-27|profoundly]] [[gifted-27|gifted]] child may be reading adult books at the age of five and showing a [[sophisticated-27|sophisticated understanding]] of abstract ideas. Such children often display intense [[inquisitiveness-27|natural inquisitiveness]], asking endless questions about how the world works.

Without appropriate challenge, these pupils may suffer. Bored by lessons that repeat what they already know, some become disruptive or lose the [[discipline-27|self-discipline]] needed for serious study. Others show [[withdrawal-27|signs of withdrawal]], avoiding classmates with whom they feel they have little in common. Because they may struggle to [[peer-27|interact with peers]] of the same age, highly able children can feel isolated, and their early promise does not always [[turn-into-27|turn into]] adult success.

Schools have developed several responses. One option is acceleration, in which a child skips a year or is allowed to [[transfer-27|transfer to another school]] with a more advanced programme. Another is an [[enriched-27|enriched programme]], which keeps students with their age group but adds deeper projects, research tasks and contact with experts. Some schemes even allow [[simultaneous-27|simultaneous]] study at school and university, so that a teenager can attend secondary classes in the morning and a university lecture in the afternoon. Whichever model is chosen, teachers must [[assess-27|carefully assess]] each child's academic and emotional readiness, since a pupil who is intellectually advanced may still be socially young.

Critics warn that separate provision for the most able can seem elitist and may draw resources away from the wider [[curriculum-27|school curriculum]]. Supporters respond that nurturing talent benefits society as a whole. What most agree on is that success depends on the adults involved. Parents and teachers who [[dedicate-27|dedicate time to]] listening, who offer [[constructive-27|constructive feedback]] rather than simple praise, and who encourage children to take risks are more likely to help talented young people reach their full potential.
