title: More Than One Bright Idea: The Story of the Electric Light
paragraphs: Few inventions have changed daily life as deeply as the electric lightbulb. Popular history often credits a single [[inventor-28|inventor]], Thomas Edison, with its creation, but the real story involves dozens of scientists and engineers working over most of the nineteenth century. The modern lightbulb was not the product of one [[inspiration-28|flash of inspiration]]; it was the result of countless experiments, business deals and legal battles.

The basic principle had been understood since the early 1800s. When an [[current-28|electric current]] passes through a thin material, the material heats up and begins to glow. The difficulty was finding a [[suitable-28|suitable material]] that would glow brightly without burning away within minutes. Early experimenters tried platinum, which was expensive, and various forms of carbon, which quickly broke apart in air. By the 1870s, several researchers, including the British chemist Joseph Swan, had produced working lamps by removing most of the air from glass bulbs, although these early [[device-28|devices]] still lasted only a short time.

Edison's contribution lay less in the original idea than in its practical development. He was an [[entrepreneur-28|entrepreneur]] as well as a scientist, and he understood that a lamp alone was of little use without a system to supply power to homes. Having persuaded wealthy [[investor-28|investors]] to [[back-28|back the project]], he set up a laboratory where his team tested thousands of materials. One [[critical-28|critical factor]] was the filament, the thin thread that actually glows. After much experimentation, the team found that carbonised bamboo, held firmly in place by a tiny [[clamp-28|clamp]], could burn for over a thousand hours. This [[refinement-28|refinement]], together with many others, made the lamp commercially practical, and Edison was soon ready to [[unveil-28|unveil his invention]] to the public.

Success quickly led to conflict. Edison [[file-28|filed]] applications to protect his design, but Swan already held a [[patent-28|patent]] in Britain, and each side suspected the other of copying. Rather than fighting a long battle over [[infringement-28|infringement]] in the British courts, the two men eventually joined forces and formed a shared company. In the United States, the situation was more bitter. Edison's lawyers pursued rival manufacturers for years, while competitors argued that his claims should be declared [[invalid-28|invalid]] because others had used similar ideas earlier. A court [[ruling-28|ruling]] in the early 1890s finally supported Edison, but by then his original [[patent-28|patent]] was close to expiring.

The competition was fierce. [[inventor-28|Inventors]] of the period feared that rivals might [[ransack-28|ransack]] their workshops in search of secret notes, and many kept their notebooks locked away. Such fears show how valuable the technology had become. Today, the ordinary lightbulb and the power networks [[specifically-28|specifically designed]] to support it [[derive-28|derive from]] the work of many people rather than one lone genius.

title: Changing the Angle: The Variable-Pitch Propeller
paragraphs: In the early decades of [[aviation-29|aviation history]], engineers faced a problem that seemed almost impossible to solve. A [[propeller-29|propeller]] works rather like a screw moving through the air: as it turns, its angled [[blade-29|blades]] push air backwards and drive the aircraft forwards. The angle of these parts, known as the [[pitch-29|pitch]], has a major effect on performance, yet on the first aeroplanes it was fixed at the factory and could not be changed during flight.

This [[inflexibility-29|inflexibility]] forced engineers into an uncomfortable compromise. A [[pitch-29|fine pitch]], in which each [[blade-29|blade]] meets the air at a shallow angle, allows the engine to turn quickly and produces strong pulling power, which is ideal for take-off and climbing. A [[coarse-29|coarse setting]], by contrast, takes a bigger "bite" of air with each [[rotation-29|rotation]] and is far more efficient once the aircraft is [[cruise-29|cruising]] at high speed. A fixed [[propeller-29|propeller]] could be good at one of these tasks but never at both, which limited the range and load of early aircraft.

A solution came largely from Wallace Rupert Turnbull, a Canadian engineer and flight [[enthusiast-29|enthusiast]]. Driven by [[curiosity-29|intellectual curiosity]], he built one of Canada's first wind tunnels near his home in New Brunswick, where he carried out [[sustained-29|sustained]] experiments on the shapes of spinning wings. Much of this research was done in relative [[isolation-29|isolation]], far from the major engineering centres of Europe and the United States. Turnbull [[design-29|designed]] a mechanism in which a small electric motor turned the [[blade-29|blades]], allowing the pilot to [[pitch-29|adjust the pitch]] while in the air. After a successful test flight in 1927, his invention was patented and later developed by a major American manufacturer.

The advantages were considerable. A [[variable-29|variable]] system could [[confer-29|confer an advantage]] at every stage of a journey: a shallow angle for a short take-off and a steep one for economical flying at altitude. Pilots found that aircraft were easier to [[handle-29|handle]] when climbing steeply or when flying through [[turbulence-29|severe turbulence]], because the engine could be kept at its most effective speed. Later versions adjusted themselves automatically, ensuring that engines performed [[reliably-29|reliably]] even during [[prolonged-29|prolonged flights]] over oceans.

Within a few years, the new technology had begun to [[revolutionize-29|revolutionize the industry]]. Airliners could carry more passengers over longer distances, and military aircraft gained speed and range that proved important during the Second World War. Although jet engines later replaced [[propeller-29|propeller]] power on most large aircraft, adjustable systems remain standard on many smaller planes today, a lasting reminder of how one engineer's patient work changed the way people travel.

title: Wiring the Ocean: The First Transatlantic Cable
paragraphs: In the mid-nineteenth century, a message sent from London to New York travelled by ship and could take ten days or more to arrive. The electric telegraph had already transformed communication on land, and engineers wondered whether a [[cable-30|cable]] could be laid across the floor of the Atlantic Ocean. Many experts considered the idea [[utterly-30|utterly impossible]]. The distance was enormous, the sea was deep, and nobody knew whether a signal could travel so far underwater.

The American businessman Cyrus Field was determined to prove them wrong. From the mid-1850s, he worked to [[rally-30|rally support]] from bankers, scientists and governments on both sides of the ocean, bringing together [[disparate-30|disparate groups]] who had rarely cooperated before. Raising the [[requisite-30|requisite funds]] was difficult, but by 1857 two warships were ready to [[set-out-30|set out]] from Ireland carrying thousands of kilometres of wire. The first attempt ended in disappointment when the line [[snap-30|snapped]] and sank to the ocean floor, and a further expedition the following year also suffered breaks.

In August 1858, the effort finally succeeded, and Queen Victoria and the American president exchanged greetings. The event was celebrated as a [[triumph-30|triumph of]] human ingenuity, with fireworks and parades in several cities. Yet the celebrations were short-lived. The signal was weak from the beginning; it took many hours to [[transmit-30|transmit]] the royal message of fewer than a hundred words. Within a few weeks, the line [[inexplicably-30|inexplicably]] stopped working altogether.

An official [[inquiry-30|inquiry]] was later launched to discover what had gone wrong. It found several problems, including a [[flaw-30|serious flaw]] in the manufacturing process and [[insulation-30|poor insulation]] that had been damaged during storage. The report also blamed the project's chief electrician, Wildman Whitehouse, who had tried to [[compensate-30|compensate for]] the weak signal by applying [[voltage-30|high voltage]] to the line. This was believed to have caused [[catastrophic-30|catastrophic damage]] to the already fragile wire. Whitehouse was [[vilified-30|widely vilified]] in the press, although some historians now argue that he was made to take too much of the blame.

Field refused to give up. The lessons of failure were applied: the new [[cable-30|cable]] was thicker, better protected and tested more carefully. In 1866, the enormous steamship Great Eastern laid a working line, and on arrival, small boats helped to [[tow-30|tow]] its heavy end ashore. The crew even recovered and repaired a section lost the previous year. This time the connection lasted, and messages that had once taken days could now be sent in minutes. Field's [[perseverance-30|sheer perseverance]] had paid off, and within decades, undersea [[cable-30|cables]] had become an [[indispensable-30|indispensable part]] of global trade and news, as they remain today.
